posts.title: The Day the Wind Turned at the Lighthouse
posts.excerpt: Guide Tomas Reyes recounts an unforgettable morning ride to the outer headland, where patience against a stiff ocean gale was rewarded by a sudden shift in the breeze.
posts.content:
We rolled out from the harbour wall at Saltmere at nine in the morning, right after our customary tyre pressure checks and luggage loading. Eight guests clipped into their pedals behind Aiko Brandt and me, while Samuel Okafor steered the white support van out toward the coast road to carry their duffels ahead. The sky hung low and silver-grey over the water, a classic overcast morning with a cool salt breeze blowing off the bay. Our destination was the outer headland, a rugged twenty-kilometre stretch of tarmac that climbs gradually toward the whitewashed lighthouse standing guard over the reef.

The second day of any coastal tour always reveals the true temperament of the sea. As we turned onto the exposed cliff lane, the wind stiffened into a stubborn headwind, pushing against our handlebars and bending the tall sea oats flat against the verge. Riding into thirty kilometres per hour of brisk maritime air requires patience rather than raw force. Aiko took the front position to break the airflow, setting an even, steady cadence of eighteen kilometres per hour that allowed all eight riders to tuck in close and conserve their legs. Nobody hurried; we kept our neat single file intact, listening to the hum of tyres on tarmac and the rhythmic clicking of gear shifts on each rise.

By noon, we had climbed the final hairpin bend and pulled into the gravel apron beneath the lighthouse. The keeper's cottage offered shelter from the gusts, and we leaned our tour bikes against the low stone boundary wall. Samuel had parked the van fifty metres down by the gate and brought up insulated flasks of hot coffee and fresh rolls from the bakery in Saltmere. We stood together with ceramic cups in our gloved hands, watching waves crash in white foam against the dark volcanic rocks sixty metres below. The wind was howling around the lantern gallery above, but everyone was smiling, buoyed by the shared accomplishment of reaching the high mark of the day.

Then, just as we packed our coffee cups back into the support crates, the weather performed the quiet miracle that coastal locals learn to watch for. The sharp whistle through the lighthouse railings abruptly died down to a gentle whisper. Out on the water, the dark lines of swell softened, and within ten minutes, the breeze swung clean around the compass from north-east to west. What had promised to be a gruelling two-hour battle against the elements for our return descent had suddenly transformed into a textbook tailwind.

Rolling away from the headland felt like taking flight. With forty kilometres of smooth tarmac stretching back toward the sheltered lagoons, the prevailing air currents pushed our small peloton forward with almost zero resistance. We barely needed to touch the big ring to maintain a brisk twenty-four kilometres per hour. Riders who had looked weary on the morning ascent were now grinning broadly as the shoreline unfurled beside us, grey-teal water glistening where faint sun broke through the cloud cover. The bikes ran silently and true, carrying us through fishing villages and across tidal causeways with effortless momentum.

We rolled into the harbour at three-thirty in the afternoon, right on schedule. Samuel's van was already parked quietly beside the guesthouse, and every guest's bag had been carried into their room forty minutes prior. Sitting on the warm harbour wall with a cold drink, listening to the halyards slapping against aluminium masts, our guests couldn't stop talking about that sudden shift at the beacon. That is the honest magic of cycling the coast: you cannot control the weather or dictate the sea, but when you ride with patience and good company, the wind eventually turns in your favour.

posts.title: Fixing a puncture in ninety seconds
posts.excerpt: Lena Vos, our mechanic, shows how a roadside puncture is mended in ninety seconds with the kit that comes with every hire bike.
posts.content:
Lena Vos runs the Saltmere workshop and fits every hire bike. Her roadside puncture routine takes about ninety seconds once the wheel is off: lever, check the tyre, new tube, a few strokes of the pump, wheel back on.

Every hire bike leaves the workshop with a repair kit, a spare tube and a mini pump. The guides carry more, and the van carries two spare bikes, but a quick fix at the roadside keeps the whole group moving.

If you would like to practise before your departure, ask Lena at the bike fitting. She is happy to hand you the tyre levers.

posts.title: Bags on the quay before we arrive
posts.excerpt: Samuel Okafor drives the van on every departure and explains how your bag reaches the next harbour before you do.
posts.content:
Samuel Okafor has driven the support van on every departure since 2016. Bags go onto the van at 08:30 each morning, one bag of up to 20 kg per guest, and by 15:00 they are standing in the hall of the next guesthouse.

He takes the coast road a little faster than the riders, stops at the harbour café to check the lunch booking and is usually on the quay with the kettle when the first bike rolls in.

It is a small thing, but it changes the day: you ride with a day bag and a clear head, and your clean clothes are already waiting.
